items.recommend_reason_zh: 从 macOS 27 和 Xcode 27 起，Apple 不再在 CodeQL 依赖的部分系统二进制和库中保留 Intel x86_64 代码，导致 CodeQL 无法在这些版本上执行 traced 扫描，也无法分析 Swift 6.4；文章建议把工作流分别固定到 macOS 26 与 Xcode 26 及更早版本，C/C++、C#、Java 可改用 build mode none 绕过。

en.reason: Apple’s macOS 27 and Xcode 27 remove Intel x86_64 code from system libraries CodeQL relies on, blocking traced scans and Swift 6.4 analysis, so pin workflows to macOS 26/Xcode 26 or use build mode none for C/C++, C#, and Java.

items.summary: 美国法院批准羁押被指控在 OpenAI 会议室安装窃听器的前工程师 Abdulrahman Alfozan。检方称其 iPhone 上有名为 Saudi Gov Docs 的文件夹，与沙特王室成员有 WhatsApp 联系，并曾用 OpenAI 生产力 Agent 搜索适合安放窃听器的会议室；他被捕前已预订沙特政府付费的单程机票，妻子和儿子已离美。

en.summary: A US court approved the detention of former engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan, who is accused of planting a listening device in an OpenAI conference room. Prosecutors say his iPhone contained a folder named Saudi Gov Docs, he had WhatsApp contacts with members of the Saudi royal family, and he used an OpenAI productivity Agent to search for conference rooms suitable for planting a listening device; before his arrest, he had booked a one-way ticket paid for by the Saudi government, and his wife and son had already left the US.
en.reason: A U.S. court ordered former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan detained after the FBI found a "Saudi Gov Docs" folder on his iPhone and alleged he used OpenAI's productivity agent to scout conference rooms for planting a listening device, while he had already booked Saudi government-paid one-way tickets to Riyadh for himself, his wife and son.

items.title: Numan 如何用 LangGraph 和 LangSmith 构建评测优先的 AI 健康教练 Nu
items.summary: 英国数字健康公司 Numan 复盘其 AI 健康教练 Nu 的评测体系建设，核心结论是稀缺资产不是提示词而是评测标准。单轮静态数据集和脚本化多轮对话都难以覆盖真实会话，Nu 改为按类别打分的主题数据集、以更廉价模型扮演患者的模拟对话层，并让安全回归自动阻断发布。

items.recommend_reason_zh: Numan 的 AI 教练 Nu 基于 LangGraph/LangSmith：单轮 eval 平均分掩盖失败、预设脚本多轮忽略真实回复，转向按类别评估与模拟对话、监管安全门。

en.summary: UK digital health company Numan has reflected on building the evaluation system for its AI health coach Nu, concluding that the scarce asset is not prompts but evaluation standards. Single-turn static datasets and scripted multi-turn dialogues struggle to cover real conversations, so Nu moved to topic datasets scored by category, a simulated-dialogue layer where cheaper models play patients, and automated blocking of releases when safety regressions occur.
en.reason: Numan’s AI health coach Nu, built on LangGraph and LangSmith, replaced single-turn static datasets and scripted multi-turn dialogues with category-scored topic datasets, simulated patient conversations using cheaper models, and safety regressions that automatically block releases.

items.title: 从 BERT、GPT 到 Jev：一文看懂大模型架构的演进与分化
items.summary: 这篇文章梳理了从原始Transformer到Decoder-only成为主流的完整技术演进，剖析了各类大模型架构的差异。或许可以帮你分清模型选型边界，快速判断自动化任务该用生成式大模型还是专用决策模型。

en.title: From BERT and GPT to Jev: Understanding the Evolution and Divergence of Large Model Architectures
en.summary: This article traces the full technical evolution from the original Transformer to the rise of Decoder-only as the mainstream, breaking down the differences among major model architectures. It may help you clarify where model selection boundaries lie and quickly determine whether an automation task calls for a generative large model or a specialized decision model.
en.reason: TypeSafe AI's September 2026 Jev skips text generation and returns probabilities for three limited question types in roughly 100 milliseconds, as the piece traces Transformer-to-BERT/GPT divergence and Decoder-only's rise.

en.title: The LLM Learning Subway Map: From Transformer to Today's Mainstream Models
en.summary: Struggling with scattered, disorganized LLM learning and fragmented knowledge? This tutorial maps the LLM knowledge system onto a subway map: one main line traces the core thread of technical evolution from Transformer to reasoning models, while five branch lines let you go deep on the directions you need. Ideal for LLM beginners looking to build a complete knowledge framework.
en.reason: A subway-map learning path with one main line and five branches traces large-model evolution from the 2017 Transformer paper to today's reasoning models, while hands-on work has readers write GPT-2 and train a small GPT on a small dataset to understand cross-entropy, backpropagation, gradient descent and Adam.

en.summary: Lovart 2.0 has launched Arti, a personal design Agent that remembers your aesthetic style and layout habits, so new projects no longer require re-entering prompts. As your body of work grows, it increasingly aligns with your creative thinking, efficiently handling batch design work such as brand visuals and cultural and creative posters.
en.reason: Lovart 2.0's personal design Agent Arti remembers accumulated aesthetic and typography habits, identifies editorial layout and Riso print texture while avoiding neon 3D chrome, and adds canvas bug inspection, one-click revisions and scheduled batch design output.

en.title: 10.12–10.19 | This Week's Top AI Papers
en.summary: This week’s 10 selected frontier AI papers span quantum circuits, long-context agents, hybrid reasoning, multi-agent collaboration, RL training optimization, and more. The research introduces multiple novel frameworks that address pain points such as agent evidence drift, context redundancy, and high compute costs, with several approaches substantially reducing token consumption and improving reasoning accuracy. Breakthroughs also include AI-assisted quantum circuit design and distributed research agents, offering developers building agent systems, tuning large models, and exploring AI-driven scientific research a highly valuable frontier reference.

en.title: For $60 a month, build an AI company.
en.summary:
For $60 a month, build your own "AI digital company": from Multi-Agent orchestration to a one-person enterprise architecture
For $60 a month, build your own "AI digital company": from Multi-Agent orchestration to a one-person enterprise architecture
For $60 a month, build your own "AI digital company": from Multi-Agent orchestration to a one-person enterprise architecture

After digging deep into GrokBotMulti-Agent orchestration recently, one thing has become increasingly clear to me: designing an efficient Multi-Agent system is essentially architecting and running a modern company. The core is the same: how, with limited resources (budget/compute), to get a group of individuals with differing strengths (employees/Agents) to jointly deliver deterministic results through sensible division of labor, processes, and rules. The only difference is that traditional management manages human employees, while we manage Agents with different model foundations, Tools, Skills, and permissions.

Below is my personal blueprint and management practice for an AI digital company.

I. Infrastructure and compute budget: the ultimate value-for-money setup at $60/month

The first step in running a company is financial planning and infrastructure. I keep the monthly budget strictly around $60, with one core principle: expensive models make decisions, cheap models execute, deterministic
en.reason: For about $60 a month, this blueprint builds an AI digital company with GPT handling decisions, a Bot as CEO, Orca orchestrating HR, finance and risk-control agents, showing Multi-Agent collaboration as enterprise-style division of labor.

Alibaba's Qwen team quietly released and open-sourced a tool that lets AI write its own code to operate a computer.

Most AI computer-use agents work step by step: look at a screenshot, click, look again. It's slow and burns through tokens.

Qwen MAI's open-source OpenGCUA is different: it lets the model decide whether to check the screen, how to act, and how to schedule tasks, and write code with loops and conditionals that mixes mouse clicks, shell commands and API calls. It can act on intermediate results without checking back with the model each time.

Early results are strong:
🔹 On OSWorld-v2, eight large models including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 gained an average 19.6 points, with 53% fewer steps.

en.reason: Alibaba's Qwen team open-sourced OpenGCUA, which lets models write their own loop-and-branch code to operate a computer instead of screenshot-click-step repetition, lifting eight large models including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 by an average 19.6 points on OSWorld-v2 while cutting steps 53%.

en.title: Can $50 break a website?
en.summary:
$50 to breach a website? AI security firm NorForge just published a chilling report: it found a Chinese-speaking hacker who, barely lifting a finger, used an AI agent and about $5,000 to break into the websites of more than 100 companies.

Backend data shows the targets included US agricultural equipment giant Deere, appliance maker SharkNinja and engine manufacturer Cummins.

The hacker gave the AI fewer than 100 Chinese characters of instructions; the rest it figured out on its own. By last weekend it had tried to attack more than 1,200 websites, with a successful breach taking about 23 hours on average.

The setup was the Claude Code framework paired with a DeepSeek AI model, burning roughly $5,000 in compute, averaging…
en.reason: NorForge reports a Chinese-speaking hacker used under 100 Chinese characters of instructions to steer Claude Code with DeepSeek, spending about $5,000 to breach 100-plus companies including Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins, after probing more than 1,200 sites.

en.title: These days plenty of people claim they can build AI Agents, when really they've just hooked up an LLM API, wired in a few tools, and wrapped the whole thing in a layer of LangGraph.
en.summary:
A lot of people now say they can build AI Agents, when in reality they've just hooked up an LLM API, called a few tools, and wrapped it in LangGraph.

Getting a demo to run makes them feel they've mastered Agent development. But put that same setup into an enterprise and have it handle real business every day, and you'll discover there's a whole pile of problems that were never solved.

I recently came across this 12-step learning roadmap for AI Agent engineers, and I think it's well worth recommending, especially for anyone aiming to move into AI Engineer, FDE, or enterprise AI deployment roles.

Because it isn't about how to quickly spin up an Agent — it's about which engineering capabilities an Agent needs to fill in before it can truly go into production.

en.title: The Origins of AI, Part 24: In 2018, why did having machines constantly predict the next word turn out to be such a powerful learning method?
en.summary:
The Origins of AI, Part 24: In 2018, why did making machines continually predict the next word become such a powerful learning method?

[24-5 · Part 2] On February 14, 2019, a group of English-speaking unicorns appeared in a news article—and the author turned out to be an AI.

How was GPT-2 able to do this? The research team further scaled up the Transformer model, having it continually practice predicting what comes next across richer internet text. Compared with GPT, which had mainly been pretrained on books, GPT-2 was exposed to a more diverse language environment. Web pages contained news reports, explanatory writing, stories, discussions, and text in many different styles, and these materials also included many examples of humans stating facts, building arguments, and narrating events.

en.title: A few days ago, we published a global Top 100 AI bloggers list, and many people asked: is there one for the Chinese-speaking community?
en.summary:
120 Chinese-language creators worth following on X in 2026 (a curated list for AI, open source, and going global)

A few days ago, I published 100 AI Accounts Worth Following on X in 2026.

After it went out, many people in the comments said lists like this are badly needed. More unexpectedly, the list helped me discover a number of excellent creators I hadn’t come across before.

So this time, I decided to go through Chinese-language X accounts separately and put together a list of Chinese creators and builders worth following long term.

I originally planned to keep it at 100.

For this list, I went through hundreds of Chinese-language accounts, checking each one’s public identity, representative work, recent posts, and the areas they’ve focused on over time. I cut and revised it for two or three days, and still ended up with 120.

I really couldn’t cut any more.

If the only goal were a tidy number, forcing out 20 more people who have actually built things wouldn’t make much sense. So this time I’m not sticking to 100; I’m keeping 120.

These 120 include not only AI bloggers but also open-source authors, indie developers, researchers, and industry analysts. The numbering is not a ranking of strength, and follower count is not a hard threshold. What I care about more is whether the person has real work, and...
en.reason: A list of 120 Chinese X creators—expanded from an intended 100 after reviewing several hundred accounts and checking public identities and representative works—covers AI, open source, going global, development and investment for long-term following.

en.title:
SIWITHUS 014 | When the entry-level ladder breaks first

This week, two things side by side: a New York report says that since ChatGPT launched, entry-level job postings in design, media, and writing are down about 40.6%, while postings requiring AI skills are up about 55%; in Anthropic’s own employment research, the share of junior technical hiring fell from 27% to 9%, and agent work hours to human hours are roughly 6 to 1.
en.reason: Entry-level design, media and writing postings fell about 40.6% since ChatGPT launched while AI-skill requirements rose 55%, and Anthropic data show junior tech hiring dropping from 27% to 9%, tracing how career ladders break before superintelligence arrives.

en.title:
Highly recommend this "stick figure animation" Agent — a must-have for launching a new account

Stick figure videos are a traffic cheat code on Douyin, YouTube, and TikTok, often pulling hundreds of thousands of views per video

I built on @CrazyKaomei's open-source project, adding automatic subtitles + final-cut quality checks, and packaged it into an Agent: type in a topic in one sentence, and storyboarding, English voiceover, generation, stitching, and subtitles are all fully automated

Tested it myself — one sentence, and a finished video in under 10 minutes. The results are genuinely impressive

Highly recommend this "stick figure animation" Agent — a must-have for launching a new account

Stick figure videos are a traffic magnet on Douyin, YouTube, and TikTok, with single videos often pulling in hundreds of thousands of views

Building on @CrazyKaomei's open-source project, I added automatic subtitles + final-video quality checks and packaged it into an Agent: enter a topic in one sentence, and storyboarding, English voiceover, generation, stitching, and subtitles are all fully automated

In testing, a single sentence produced a finished video in under 10 minutes — the results are genuinely impressive

Install and go: https://t.co/l28sKBUUN8
en.reason: Built on @CrazyKaomei's open-source stick-figure animation project, this Agent adds automatic subtitles and footage quality checks, turning a one-sentence topic into storyboards, English narration, rendering, stitching and captions, with a tested output in under 10 minutes.

en.title: If you've been feeling lost lately, or you keep thinking "I'm working hard but it's all internal friction," go take Dan Koe's Human 3.0 test. The framework comes from the famous "godfather of the super-individual" @thedankoe, who has zero employees and earns millions of dollars a year from personal digital assets alone: in the game of life, there are really only three ways to live. 1.0 The Conformist (NPC): your life is entirely scripted by outside forces.
en.reason: Dan Koe's (@thedankoe) Human 3.0 splits life into three modes—1.0 NPCs, 2.0 ascetics chasing money—and flags hoarding tips to avoid publishing as false effort, from a creator earning millions yearly with no employees.

en.title: Seeing so many people enjoy this game demo puts my mind at ease. That said, Codex+Unreal isn't the optimal solution—Unreal built a skill specifically for Claude Code, which gives Claude a higher development ceiling. We have hit some bottlenecks, though: LLMs can't handle Control Rig well, especially complex attack animations. Anyone got a good solution?
en.reason: A game demo drawing positive reactions faces a development bottleneck: Unreal has built a dedicated skill for Claude Code, yet large language models still fail at Control Rig work like complex attack animations, and the developer is asking the community for solutions.

en.title: Most people have the wrong idea about how AI ultimately plays out.
en.reason: AI is cast as biological evolution, with LLMs as DNA instruction sets and embodied AI as cell differentiation and body formation, while today’s systems are only fertilized—not embryos—and real AGI’s physical carrier remains the question.

en.title: Having only used GPT, Claude, and Kimi K3, here’s my personal take: GPT is in a league of its own on instruction following, handling edge cases and complex logic better.
en.summary:
I've only used GPT, Claude, and Kimi K3, so here are my personal views:

GPT is in a league of its own when it comes to instruction following, and it handles edge cases and complex logic better. But the cost is frequent over-caution and over-engineering—it nitpicks endlessly like a lawyer. If you have a very detailed spec, GPT can execute it perfectly in one shot without missing a thing. But none of GPT's current models sound very human, and 6.1 Sol is unbearably slow.

Also, GPT's instruction following is too rigid. For example, if you ask it to find bugs, it won't come back and say the project has no bugs—it'll force itself to find some edge-case bug. So collaborating with it is a terrible experience; you constantly have to guess how GPT will interpret your instructions and write your instructions so they're watertight.

Claude is the most human-like model; it is...
en.reason: GPT's instruction-following is called a class apart for edge cases, but 6.1 Sol is absurdly slow, GPT models sound robotic, and asking for bugs yields invented ones, in a user's comparison of GPT, Claude and Kimi K3.

items_ai.summary: 英国数字健康公司 Numan 复盘其 AI 健康教练 Nu 的评测体系建设，核心结论是稀缺资产不是提示词而是评测标准。单轮静态数据集和脚本化多轮对话都难以覆盖真实会话，Nu 改为按类别打分的主题数据集、以更廉价模型扮演患者的模拟对话层，并让安全回归自动阻断发布。

en.summary: UK digital health company Numan has reflected on building the evaluation system for its AI health coach Nu, concluding that the scarce asset is not prompts but evaluation standards. Single-turn static datasets and scripted multi-turn dialogues struggle to cover real conversations, so Nu moved to topic datasets scored by category, a simulated-dialogue layer where cheaper models play patients, and automated blocking of releases when safety regressions occur.
en.reason: Numan’s AI health coach Nu, built on LangGraph and LangSmith, replaced single-turn static datasets and scripted multi-turn dialogues with category-scored topic datasets, simulated patient conversations using cheaper models, and safety regressions that automatically block releases.

After digging deep into GrokBotMulti-Agent orchestration recently, one thing has become increasingly clear to me: designing an efficient Multi-Agent system is essentially architecting and running a modern company. The core is the same: how, with limited resources (budget/compute), to get a group of individuals with differing strengths (employees/Agents) to jointly deliver deterministic results through sensible division of labor, processes, and rules. The only difference is that traditional management manages human employees, while we manage Agents with different model foundations, Tools, Skills, and permissions.

en.title: 💥 Incredible!
en.summary:
Alibaba's Qwen team quietly released and open-sourced a tool that lets AI write its own code to operate a computer.

Most AI computer-use agents work step by step: look at a screenshot, click, look again. It's slow and burns through tokens.

Qwen MAI's open-source OpenGCUA is different: it lets the model decide whether to check the screen, how to act, and how to schedule tasks, and write code with loops and conditionals that mixes mouse clicks, shell commands and API calls. It can act on intermediate results without checking back with the model each time.

Early results are strong:
🔹 On OSWorld-v2, eight large models including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 gained an average 19.6 points, with 53% fewer steps.
🔹 It also ships a cross-device SDK (ele…
en.reason: Alibaba's Qwen team open-sourced OpenGCUA, which lets models write their own loop-and-branch code to operate a computer instead of screenshot-click-step repetition, lifting eight large models including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 by an average 19.6 points on OSWorld-v2 while cutting steps 53%.

en.title: Can $50 break a website?
en.summary:
$50 to breach a website? AI security firm NorForge just published a chilling report: it found a Chinese-speaking hacker who, barely lifting a finger, used an AI agent and about $5,000 to break into the websites of more than 100 companies.

Backend data shows the targets included US agricultural equipment giant Deere, appliance maker SharkNinja and engine manufacturer Cummins.

The hacker gave the AI fewer than 100 Chinese characters of instructions; the rest it figured out on its own. By last weekend it had tried to attack more than 1,200 websites, with a successful breach taking about 23 hours on average.

The setup was the Claude Code framework paired with a DeepSeek AI model, burning roughly $5,000 in compute, averaging…
en.reason: NorForge reports a Chinese-speaking hacker used under 100 Chinese characters of instructions to steer Claude Code with DeepSeek, spending about $5,000 to breach 100-plus companies including Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins, after probing more than 1,200 sites.

en.title: These days plenty of people claim they can build AI Agents, when really they've just hooked up an LLM API, wired in a few tools, and wrapped the whole thing in a layer of LangGraph.
en.summary:
A lot of people now say they can build AI Agents, when in reality they've just hooked up an LLM API, called a few tools, and wrapped it in LangGraph.

Getting a demo to run makes them feel they've mastered Agent development. But put that same setup into an enterprise and have it handle real business every day, and you'll discover there's a whole pile of problems that were never solved.

I recently came across this 12-step learning roadmap for AI Agent engineers, and I think it's well worth recommending, especially for anyone aiming to move into AI Engineer, FDE, or enterprise AI deployment roles.

Because it isn't about how to quickly spin up an Agent — it's about which engineering capabilities an Agent needs to fill in before it can truly go into production.

en.title: The Origins of AI, Part 24: In 2018, why did having machines constantly predict the next word turn out to be such a powerful learning method?
en.summary:
The Origins of AI, Part 24: In 2018, why did making machines continually predict the next word become such a powerful learning method?

[24-5 · Part 2] On February 14, 2019, a group of English-speaking unicorns appeared in a news article—and the author turned out to be an AI.

How was GPT-2 able to do this? The research team further scaled up the Transformer model, having it continually practice predicting what comes next across richer internet text. Compared with GPT, which had mainly been pretrained on books, GPT-2 was exposed to a more diverse language environment. Web pages contained news reports, explanatory writing, stories, discussions, and text in many different styles, and these materials also included many examples of humans stating facts, building arguments, and narrating events.

en.title: A few days ago, we published a global Top 100 AI bloggers list, and many people asked: is there one for the Chinese-speaking community?
en.summary:
120 Chinese-language creators worth following on X in 2026 (a curated list for AI, open source, and going global)

A few days ago, I published 100 AI Accounts Worth Following on X in 2026.

After it went out, many people in the comments said lists like this are badly needed. More unexpectedly, the list helped me discover a number of excellent creators I hadn’t come across before.

So this time, I decided to go through Chinese-language X accounts separately and put together a list of Chinese creators and builders worth following long term.

I originally planned to keep it at 100.

For this list, I went through hundreds of Chinese-language accounts, checking each one’s public identity, representative work, recent posts, and the areas they’ve focused on over time. I cut and revised it for two or three days, and still ended up with 120.

I really couldn’t cut any more.

If the only goal were a tidy number, forcing out 20 more people who have actually built things wouldn’t make much sense. So this time I’m not sticking to 100; I’m keeping 120.

These 120 include not only AI bloggers but also open-source authors, indie developers, researchers, and industry analysts. The numbering is not a ranking of strength, and follower count is not a hard threshold. What I care about more is whether the person has real work, and...
en.reason: A list of 120 Chinese X creators—expanded from an intended 100 after reviewing several hundred accounts and checking public identities and representative works—covers AI, open source, going global, development and investment for long-term following.

en.title:
SIWITHUS 014 | When the entry-level ladder breaks first

This week, two things side by side: a New York report says that since ChatGPT launched, entry-level job postings in design, media, and writing are down about 40.6%, while postings requiring AI skills are up about 55%; in Anthropic’s own employment research, the share of junior technical hiring fell from 27% to 9%, and agent work hours to human hours are roughly 6 to 1.
en.reason: Entry-level design, media and writing postings fell about 40.6% since ChatGPT launched while AI-skill requirements rose 55%, and Anthropic data show junior tech hiring dropping from 27% to 9%, tracing how career ladders break before superintelligence arrives.

In testing, a single sentence produced a finished video in under 10 minutes — the results are genuinely impressive

Install and go: https://t.co/l28sKBUUN8
en.reason: Built on @CrazyKaomei's open-source stick-figure animation project, this Agent adds automatic subtitles and footage quality checks, turning a one-sentence topic into storyboards, English narration, rendering, stitching and captions, with a tested output in under 10 minutes.

en.summary:
I've only used GPT, Claude, and Kimi K3, so here are my personal views:

GPT is in a league of its own when it comes to instruction following, and it handles edge cases and complex logic better. But the cost is frequent over-caution and over-engineering—it nitpicks endlessly like a lawyer. If you have a very detailed spec, GPT can execute it perfectly in one shot without missing a thing. But none of GPT's current models sound very human, and 6.1 Sol is unbearably slow.

Also, GPT's instruction following is too rigid. For example, if you ask it to find bugs, it won't come back and say the project has no bugs—it'll force itself to find some edge-case bug. So collaborating with it is a terrible experience; you constantly have to guess how GPT will interpret your instructions and write your instructions so they're watertight.
